title: The valley spirit
hook: the valley spirit never dies; it is the mysterious female (Tao Te Ching 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, straw dogs, and your line was not personal. Did you get to say it to a red light or a spill? Chapter six goes looking for the lowest ground. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

Hikers climb the peak for the view, take the photograph, and head back down. Nobody stays up there. The farms are below, in the valley: the river, the deep soil, the orchards, the villages, the smoke from kitchen chimneys. The high place is admired. The low place is where things grow. Chapter six of the Tao Te Ching is barely a few lines long, and it chooses the valley as its picture of something that never dies.
screen: `THE PEAK GETS THE VIEW.` → `THE VALLEY GETS THE FARMS.` → `THE LOW PLACE IS WHERE THINGS GROW.`

segments.voice: First, the valley never dies. Legge put this chapter into rhyming verse, and it begins: "The valley spirit dies not, aye the same." A valley is a hollow. It's defined by what isn't there. And because it's low and open, it keeps receiving: rain, snowmelt, rivers. It doesn't wear out. Second, the mysterious female. The chapter names the valley spirit the mysterious female, the dark mother. Here the book reaches for a picture of birth: the Tao not as a ruler giving orders from above, but as a mother from whom everything comes, low and hidden and endlessly giving. Third, its gate is the root. The chapter says the gate of this mysterious female is the root of heaven and earth. That's the third gate in a week: the border gate of the story, the gate of the mystery in chapter one, and now this one. Each time, the gate is an opening, not a wall. One old commentary, traditionally credited to a figure called Heshang Gong, reads the chapter in the body: it hears the valley as nourishing the spirit, and the gate of the mysterious female as the nose and mouth, where breath comes and goes. Other readers keep it as a picture of the world. Fourth, used gently. The chapter ends by saying this power goes on unbroken, used gently, without strain. The valley never forces anything. It just stays low and open, and the water arrives.
screen: `THE VALLEY NEVER DIES.` · `THE MYSTERIOUS FEMALE.` · `ITS GATE IS THE ROOT.` · `USED GENTLY, WITHOUT STRAIN.` · then, large: `THE VALLEY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to rest in a low place. If you can, get low: sit on the floor, or lie down, or lean back so your body sinks. Let the floor take your weight. Breathe gently, without strain, through the nose. Notice the breath arriving on its own, the way water arrives in a valley without being called. You don't have to pull it in. Just stay low and open, and let it come. If you pray, you can pray from this low place. If you don't, simply rest there. The bell holds the time.
The valley spirit. Chapter six's picture of what never dies: low, open, receiving, the mysterious female whose gate is the root of heaven and earth. Today's word.
Your line: the valley. Once today, when you'd usually rise up to win a point, stay low instead, and let what's coming arrive. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Taoist practitioners connect chapter six with gentle breathing practice, following an old commentary that reads the gate of the mysterious female as the nose and mouth; other readers take it as a picture of the world's source.

notes: Legge renders chapter 6 in verse; the first line is quoted. Please verify exact wording and punctuation against the 1891 text.

Heshang Gong reading (谷 as 'to nourish'; the gate of the mysterious female as nose and mouth) is paraphrased from memory of the commentary; a Keeper should confirm before release. The commentary's attribution and date are left out on purpose.
'Barely a few lines long' (hook) describes chapter 6's length; confirm.
'Third gate in a week' refers to days 1062 (border gate), 1063 (gate of the mystery, ch. 1) and today.

Editor pass: hook no longer opens on rain running downhill (rain led yesterday's hook and water leads 1070); now the peak's view against the valley's farms. 'Without strain' is no longer attributed to Legge's verse, which reads 'without the touch of pain'.
